title: Values, equality and coercion
summary: How JavaScript copies primitives but shares objects, what `typeof` really reports, how `==`, `===` and `Object.is` differ, which values are falsy, when `??` beats `||`, and the number and sort gotchas TypeScript helps you catch.
prerequisiteNotes: Comfort with `let`/`const`, functions and closures from ts-scope-closures. No prior knowledge of the coercion rules is assumed.
objectives: Explain that primitives are copied by value while objects are shared by reference, and why `{} === {}` is false.
Walk through the abstract equality (`==`) algorithm for null, booleans, number/string pairs and objects, and say when `Object.is` differs from `===`.
List the eight falsy values and choose `??` over `||` whenever 0, `""` or `false` are legitimate values.
Avoid the number and sort traps: float sums, unsafe integers, global `isNaN`, and `sort()` without a comparator.

concepts.title: Primitives are values, objects are references
concepts.body: JavaScript has seven primitive types: `string`, `number`, `bigint`, `boolean`, `undefined`, `symbol` and `null`. Primitives are immutable and compared by value, so assigning one copies the value. Everything else (arrays, functions, plain objects, Maps) is an **object**: a variable holds a reference, `b = a` shares it, and `===` compares identity, so two separately built `{ n: 1 }` are never equal. Arguments work the same way (pass by sharing): mutating a parameter object is visible to the caller, reassigning the parameter is not. `Symbol("id") !== Symbol("id")`: each symbol is unique even though it is a primitive.
concepts.code:
const a = { n: 1 }
const b = a            // same object, two names
b.n = 2
console.log(a.n)       // 2
const c = { n: 2 }
console.log(a === b, a === c)  // true false
let x = 5
let y = x              // copies the value
y++
console.log(x, y)      // 5 6

concepts.title: `typeof` quirks and the eight falsy values
concepts.body: `typeof null` is `"object"` (a bug kept for compatibility), `typeof` a function is `"function"`, and arrays are just `"object"`, so use `Array.isArray`. `typeof 10n` is `"bigint"` and `typeof Symbol()` is `"symbol"`. Exactly eight values are **falsy**: `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `""`, `null`, `undefined` and `NaN`. Everything else is truthy, including `"0"`, `"false"`, `[]`, `{}` and `new Boolean(false)`. Unlike Python, an empty array is truthy, so test `arr.length === 0`.

concepts.title: `===`, `==` and `Object.is`
concepts.body: `===` (strict equality) never converts: different types are unequal, objects compare by identity. `==` (abstract equality) converts first: `null` and `undefined` equal each other and nothing else; a boolean becomes a number; in a number/string pair the string becomes a number; an object compared with a primitive is turned into a primitive (`valueOf`, then `toString`; arrays join with commas). Then it compares again. `Object.is` is `===` with two fixes: `Object.is(NaN, NaN)` is true and `Object.is(0, -0)` is false. `includes`, `Map` and `Set` use SameValueZero (finds NaN, treats ±0 as equal); `indexOf` uses `===` and never finds NaN.
concepts.code:
console.log(0 === -0, Object.is(0, -0))        // true false
console.log([NaN].indexOf(NaN), [NaN].includes(NaN)) // -1 true
const v: unknown = null
console.log(v == undefined, v === undefined)    // true false
// the one common deliberate use of ==: x == null catches null and undefined

concepts.title: `??` versus `||`, and optional chaining
concepts.body: `a || b` returns `b` whenever `a` is **falsy**, so a real `0`, `""` or `false` is silently replaced. `a ?? b` (nullish coalescing) falls back only for `null` or `undefined`; `??=` assigns only when the target is nullish. You cannot mix `??` with `||`/`&&` without parentheses (it is a SyntaxError). Optional chaining `a?.b.c`, `a?.[k]` and `fn?.()` stops the whole chain and yields `undefined` as soon as the value before `?.` is nullish; it does not swallow errors further down, and it cannot be an assignment target.

concepts.title: Number and sort gotchas
concepts.body: Every `number` is an IEEE 754 double: `0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004`, and integers are exact only up to `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` (2^53 - 1), so `2 ** 53 === 2 ** 53 + 1`. Use integer cents or `bigint` (`10n`) for exact maths; mixing `bigint` and `number` in arithmetic throws a TypeError. Global `isNaN("abc")` coerces and returns true; `Number.isNaN` does not coerce. `Number("12px")` is NaN but `parseInt("12px", 10)` is 12, and `Number("")` is 0. Finally, `sort()` with no comparator converts elements to strings and orders by UTF-16 code units, so `[10, 9, 1].sort()` gives `[1, 10, 9]`. It also sorts in place; `toSorted` (ES2023) returns a copy.
concepts.code:
console.log(0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3, Math.abs(0.1 + 0.2 - 0.3) < Number.EPSILON)  // false true
console.log(Number.isSafeInteger(2 ** 53))    // false
console.log(2n ** 64n)                         // 18446744073709551616n
console.log(Number.isNaN('abc'))               // false
console.log([10, 9, 1].toSorted((a, b) => a - b).join(','))  // 1,9,10

walkthrough.title: Implementing `==` by hand
walkthrough.body: Order the checks the way the algorithm resolves them. Handle `null` first, because `typeof null` is `"object"` and would otherwise be treated as an object. Next, if both sides have the same `typeof`, the answer is just `===`. Otherwise convert one side and **recurse**: a boolean becomes a number, a string facing a number becomes a number, an object facing a primitive becomes a string via `String(obj)`. Recursion is what makes `[] == false` true: false becomes 0, `[]` becomes `""`, and `""` becomes 0.

walkthrough.title: Let TypeScript catch the trap
walkthrough.body: Under `strict`, many of these bugs never compile. `1 == "1"` with known types is error TS2367 (the types have no overlap); `x === NaN` is TS2845, which suggests `Number.isNaN`; `1n + 1` is rejected; `strictNullChecks` forces you to handle `undefined` before using a value, which pushes you toward `?.` and `??`. When a snippet needs the loose behaviour on purpose, route the value through `unknown` or mark the line with `// @ts-expect-error`, which also fails the build if the error ever disappears. TypeScript does **not** catch `||` swallowing 0, or `sort()` without a comparator on numbers.

task: Write `looseEqual(a, b)` for JSON values (`null`, booleans, numbers, strings, arrays and plain objects) that returns exactly what `a == b` would, without using `==` or `!=`. Two separate arrays or objects are never equal; an array compared with a primitive is first turned into its comma-joined string, and a plain object into `"[object Object]"`.
hints: Check `null` before anything else: `typeof null` is `"object"`, and null is only loosely equal to null (or undefined).
When the `typeof`s differ, convert exactly one side (boolean → `Number`, string facing a number → `Number`, object → `String`) and call `looseEqual` again.
checklist: I handle `null` before relying on `typeof` returning `"object"`.
Same-type comparisons use `===`, so two distinct arrays are unequal.
Booleans are converted to numbers before any other conversion.
Objects become primitives with `String(...)` and the comparison recurses.
pitfalls: Using `||` for defaults when 0, `""` or `false` are valid values; use `??`.
Testing `typeof x === "object"` and forgetting that null passes; arrays pass too.
Calling `nums.sort()` on numbers and getting string order.
Expecting `{ a: 1 } === { a: 1 }` or `[1] === [1]` to be true.
Summing money as floats, or using numbers above 2^53 - 1 as IDs.

extraPractice.title: Defaults that respect zero
extraPractice.prompt: Write `resolveSettings(input)` where every field of `{ retries, label, verbose }` may be missing or `null`. Fill in defaults 3, `"default"` and `true`, but keep any value the caller actually supplied, including `0`, `""` and `false`.
checklist: Missing and null fields both get the default.

extraPractice.title: Exact money sums
extraPractice.prompt: Write `addMoney(amounts)` that adds decimal strings such as `"12"`, `"0.1"` or `"-3.07"` (at most two decimals) and returns the exact total with exactly two decimals, e.g. `"0.30"`. An empty list gives `"0.00"`. Totals may exceed `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` cents.
hints: Parse each amount into whole cents as a `bigint` so nothing is rounded.
Format at the end: sign, `abs / 100n`, a dot, and `abs % 100n` padded to two digits.
checklist: Negative totals keep their sign, including "-0.05".

followUps.question: Why is `[] == ![]` true?
followUps.answer: `![]` is `false` because every object is truthy. Then `[] == false`: the boolean becomes 0, the array becomes the primitive `""` (empty join), and `""` becomes 0, so `0 === 0`. It is a neat demonstration that `==` is not even consistent with truthiness.

followUps.question: Is there ever a good reason to use `==`?
followUps.answer: One: `x == null` is true for exactly `null` and `undefined`, a compact nullish check that many lint configs allow (`eqeqeq` with the null exception). Everywhere else use `===`, so reviewers never have to run the coercion algorithm in their heads.

followUps.question: How would you compare two objects for equality?
followUps.answer: There is no built-in deep equality. Write a recursive structural compare (same key set, equal values, `Object.is` for leaves if NaN matters) or use a tested library. `JSON.stringify(a) === JSON.stringify(b)` is fragile: key order matters, `undefined` and functions vanish, NaN becomes null, and Maps serialize as `{}`.

followUps.question: How do you handle IDs larger than 2^53?
followUps.answer: Keep them as strings end to end, or parse to `bigint` when you need arithmetic. `JSON.parse` turns large numeric literals into rounded doubles, so a 64-bit ID from an API must arrive as a string to stay exact.

takeaways: Primitives are copied by value; objects are shared by reference and `===` compares identity.
Exactly eight values are falsy: false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined and NaN.
Use `===` everywhere, `x == null` at most, and `Object.is` when NaN or -0 matter.
`??` defaults only on null/undefined; `||` also clobbers 0, "" and false.
Doubles are inexact past 2^53 - 1 and for most decimals; `sort()` without a comparator compares strings.

diagrams.title: Shared object, copied number
diagrams.alt: Memory diagram. Variables a and b both point to one object holding n: 2. Variable c points to a different object that also holds n: 2. Variables x and y each hold their own copy of a number, 5 and 6.
diagrams.caption: Objects are shared through references and compared by identity; primitives are copied, so changing y never touches x.

steps.text: `b = a` copies the reference, not the object. `b.n = 2` changes the one object both names reach, so `a.n` is 2 and `a === b` is true.
`c` points at a different object with the same contents. `a === c` is false: `===` on objects compares identity, never contents.
Numbers are primitives. `y = x` copies the value 5, so `y++` changes only y.

diagrams.title: The eight falsy values, by typeof
diagrams.alt: Bar chart counting falsy values per typeof result. number has three (0, -0, NaN); bigint, string, boolean, undefined and object (null) have one each. Eight in total.
diagrams.caption: Memorise the list, not a rule: three numbers plus one each of 0n, "", false, undefined and null. Every other value, including [] and "0", is truthy.

diagrams.title: How a == b decides
diagrams.alt: Decision flow for abstract equality. If both sides have the same type, use strict equality. If either side is null or undefined, the result is true only when both are. A boolean side becomes a number. In a number and string pair the string becomes a number. An object facing a primitive becomes a primitive. Each conversion loops back to compare again; anything else is false.
diagrams.caption: Every conversion moves one side towards a number and compares again. That recursion is why [] == false ends up as 0 === 0.

steps.text: Same type: `==` behaves exactly like `===`. Two arrays are equal only if they are the same array.
`null == undefined` is true, but `null == 0` and `null == false` are false: null is not converted to a number here.
A boolean side is converted first: `"1" == true` becomes `"1" == 1`, then the string rule applies.
Number versus string: the string becomes a number, so `"" == 0` and `" 12 " == 12` are both true.
Object versus primitive: `[1, 2] == "1,2"` is true because the array joins to "1,2". A plain object becomes "[object Object]".
Anything left over (for example a symbol versus a number) is false.

diagrams.title: Defaults with || versus ??
diagrams.alt: Side-by-side comparison. With x || 8080, the inputs 0, empty string and null all fall through to the default 8080. With x ?? 8080, 0 and the empty string are kept and only null falls through to 8080.
diagrams.caption: || treats every falsy value as missing. ?? treats only null and undefined as missing, so deliberate zeros and empty strings survive.

diagrams.title: Why [10, 9, 1].sort() gives [1, 10, 9]
diagrams.alt: Sequence diagram. Code calls sort on the array 10, 9, 1 with no comparator. Sort converts each element to a string and compares them by UTF-16 code units, so "10" sorts before "9". The array is mutated to 1, 10, 9. A second call with the comparator (a, b) => a - b returns 1, 9, 10.
diagrams.caption: Always pass a comparator for numbers. Without one, sort compares strings character by character.

messages.label: compare '10' and '9'
messages.note: Each element is converted with String(); undefined is moved to the end.
Strings compare by UTF-16 code units, first character first.
Sorted in place: the original array is mutated and returned.
Negative: a first. Positive: b first. Zero: keep order (sort is stable).

predict.explain: `typeof null` is the historical "object" bug, arrays are objects (use `Array.isArray`), functions get their own "function" tag, and bigint literals report "bigint".

predict.code:
// @ts-expect-error -- TS2367: number and string have no overlap
const a = 0 == ''
const b = (null as unknown) == 0
const c = (null as unknown) == undefined
// @ts-expect-error -- string and number[] have no overlap
const d = '1,2' == [1, 2]
console.log(a, b, c, d)
predict.explain: `""` becomes 0, so `0 == ""`. null loosely equals only null and undefined, so `null == 0` is false. The array becomes the string "1,2". Note that TypeScript rejects two of these lines outright: that is the compiler protecting you.
`||` replaces any falsy value, so 0 → 10 and "" → "none". `??` replaces only null/undefined, so the deliberate 0 and "" are kept.

predict.code:
const x = NaN
// @ts-expect-error -- TS2845: this condition will always return 'false'
const same = x === NaN
console.log(same, Object.is(x, NaN), 0 === -0, Object.is(0, -0))
predict.explain: NaN is never `===` to anything, itself included; TypeScript even flags the comparison and suggests `Number.isNaN`. `Object.is` fixes both edge cases: NaN equals NaN, and 0 differs from -0.

Without a comparator, elements are compared as strings: "1" < "10" < "100" < "9". `sort` mutates in place and returns the same array, so `sorted === nums`. Use `toSorted((a, b) => a - b)` for a sorted copy.
0.1 and 0.2 are not exact in binary. 2^53 + 1 is not representable as a double and rounds back to 2^53. `Number.isNaN` does not coerce, so the string "abc" is simply not NaN.
`b = a` shares the reference, so the write is visible through a. The spread made a new (shallow) copy before the write, so c keeps 1 and is a different object.

lab.tip: When an interviewer shows a `==` puzzle, narrate the algorithm out loud ("boolean to number, array to primitive, string to number") instead of guessing, then say you would write `===` and let TypeScript reject the comparison. For defaults, say "?? because 0 is valid" before they ask.
